So Why Do We Build Products Around Problems? Aadithyan Ammencheril 3 min read · Just now -- Listen Share There is a recurring idea in product management that building a product should begin with identifying a problem. We are taught that empathy is the first step in design thinking, that we must understand the user, identify their pain points, formulate a problem statement and then work towards a solution. While I understand the reasoning behind this approach, I have often wondered whether we have reduced innovation to problem-solving. Did anyone ask for an iPhone before it existed? Did people know they needed a conversational interface to interact with artificial intelligence before ChatGPT became accessible? Did people anticipate how social networking would evolve before Facebook? Perhaps not. And yet, these products went on to change how we interact with technology and, in many ways, with each other. I think there is more to innovation than identifying an existing problem. There are two ways to approach innovation. One begins with a problem; the other begins with a possibility. The first is what we commonly understand as problem-led innovation. We observe an existing situation, identify something that isn’t working, understand the people affected by it and develop a solution. This is particularly useful when improving existing products, addressing customer friction or entering an established market. The second begins with a technological advancement, an emerging opportunity or an idea about what might be possible. It does not necessarily start with a clearly articulated customer need. Instead, it explores what a new capability could enable and, eventually, how people might find value in it. Consider generative AI. Before ChatGPT, people certainly wanted help with writing, programming, learning and information retrieval. However, they did not necessarily imagine a single interface that could assist with all these activities through natural language. The technology made a new experience possible, and that experience subsequently revealed applications and use cases that were not previously obvious. In this case, innovation did not simply respond to demand. It also created it. This distinction is important because people are generally better at describing their existing experiences than imagining experiences they have never encountered. Asking someone what they want from a technology that does not yet exist may only produce answers shaped by what they already know. This is not to suggest that empathy or problem statements are unnecessary. In fact, they are essential in understanding whether an opportunity can translate into something valuable. They help us distinguish between what we assume people need and what they actually need. They also prevent us from becoming so attached to a solution that we overlook whether it serves any meaningful purpose. However, the limitation arises when we treat problem-first thinking as a universal principle rather than one approach to innovation. A narrowly defined problem can sometimes restrict the possibilities we explore. We might become occupied with improving an existing experience without questioning whether that experience itself can be reimagined. We might also overlook technological opportunities simply because customers have not articulated a demand for them. There is another distinction worth considering. Product development and innovation are related, but they are not necessarily the same thing. Product management often deals with translating opportunities into products that create value for users and businesses. Innovation, however, can begin much earlier, with the discovery of something that changes what is possible. Perhaps the more appropriate approach is not to insist that every product must begin with a problem statement, but to understand where the opportunity originates. It could be an existing customer problem, a technological breakthrough, a change in consumer behaviour, an emerging market or even a conviction about how the future should look. Each requires a different starting point, and each eventually needs to confront the same questions: Who benefits? Is the proposition valuable? Is it technically feasible? Is there a sustainable way to deliver it? A problem statement is useful in bringing clarity to these questions. But it should not become a constraint on the questions we are willing to ask. I find this particularly relevant as we enter an era where technological capabilities are evolving faster than our ability to understand their applications. We may not always know what to ask for, what to build or even what problems a new technology could address.
